passage: On Sunday night the hostel study hall still had one lamp burning. Shalini had not opened a book since the term began, and the chemistry test was on Monday. She stacked six chapters on the desk and read until the sweepers came at dawn. Her friend Jyoti brought tea twice and said, "Sleep a little." "Fourteen hours today, that's my record," Shalini said, grinning. On Monday she wrote the test with a headache and mixed up two reactions. By Wednesday she stared at the ceiling instead of the textbook, and she skipped study hall for the whole next week. When Jyoti asked about the notes, Shalini shrugged. "I know the first three chapters and half of the fifth. The rest is fog."

qa.q: How long did Shalini say she had studied that Sunday?
qa.a: Shalini said she studied fourteen hours and called it her record.

qa.q: What was Shalini feeling as she grinned about her record?
qa.a: She felt proud and a little heroic, though the headache and the mixed-up reactions on Monday show the cost.

qa.q: What could Shalini try before the next test instead?
qa.a: She could study for a shorter stretch on most days so chapters never pile up, and rest in between so she can keep it going.

qa.q: How might Jyoti feel watching Shalini skip study hall for a whole week?
qa.a: Jyoti is probably worried, since Jyoti had already urged Shalini to sleep and now sees the studying stop altogether.

grounding: Illustrates a teenager who crams for hours after weeks of little study, then burns out and leaves knowledge patchy.

passage:
Dear Pooja,
You asked how my exams went, so here is the honest version. For six weeks I did almost nothing. Then, four days before the maths paper, I studied fourteen hours straight on Saturday, with only two breaks for water. I felt unstoppable. On Sunday I slept till noon, and on Monday I could not even open the textbook. I told Amma I would "catch up next week" and then I did not touch it for seven days. In the paper I remembered the algebra I had crammed and blanked on the geometry I never looked at. I keep telling myself that big Saturday proves I work hard, but honestly my knowledge is patchy. This week I am trying forty minutes a day. Boring, but I can repeat it. Write back and tell me what works for you.
Ishita

qa.q: How many hours did Ishita study on the Saturday before the maths paper?
qa.a: Ishita studied fourteen hours, with only two breaks for water.

qa.q: What does Ishita feel about that big Saturday when looking back?
qa.a: Mixed feelings: some pride in the effort, but unease, since the paper showed patchy knowledge and a whole week was lost.

qa.q: What small change is Ishita trying now, and why might it last?
qa.a: Ishita is trying forty minutes a day, which is small enough to repeat, unlike the exhausting Saturday.

qa.q: How might Pooja feel on reading this letter?
qa.a: Pooja is probably concerned but glad Ishita was so honest, since the letter ends by asking Pooja for advice.

grounding: Illustrates a teenager who studied in one huge burst, collapsed for a week and ended up with uneven knowledge.

passage:
Subject: Day two, and the end of my plan
Hi Seema,
You asked how the new routine is going, so: it isn't. On the first of January I woke at five, ran three laps of the campus ground, did two hours of revision and ticked every box on a chart. On day two my alarm rang and I slept through it. I looked at the empty box and thought, that's it, the streak is dead. By evening I had peeled the chart off the wall, skipped the run, the revision and dinner in the mess, and eaten biscuits in bed. It has been ten days. One bad morning should not have wiped out everything, but at the time it felt like all or nothing. Maybe I'll try again on Monday with a smaller plan. Tell me I'm not hopeless. 🙂
Wasim

qa.q: What did Wasim do on the first of January before revising?
qa.a: Wasim woke at five and ran three laps of the campus ground.

qa.q: What was Wasim thinking when looking at the empty box on the chart?
qa.a: That the streak was dead and the whole plan was ruined, a discouraged all-or-nothing thought.

qa.q: What could Wasim change in the plan for Monday?
qa.a: Make it smaller and allow one missed morning without dropping everything else, so a slip stays a slip.

qa.q: How might Seema read the line asking to be told Wasim is not hopeless?
qa.a: As a request for reassurance. Seema would likely see someone discouraged rather than lazy and may reply kindly. 😊

grounding: Illustrates a young adult who starts an ambitious routine and abandons it after one missed morning.

passage: So, Parveen, here is my confession for this year, from Anand the timetable person. On the first of January I made a timetable for my final-year project: five hours of coding every day, no phone, in bed by ten, colour-coded. I did it perfectly for nine days. On day ten my cousin's wedding ran late and I got home at two. I skipped the morning session, and by afternoon I was telling myself, well, the streak's gone, might as well start fresh in February. February became March. The funny part is that all I had really missed was one day. If I had just opened the laptop for twenty minutes that evening, the whole thing would have kept going. Now I do a plain thirty minutes and the code is actually moving.

qa.q: How long did Anand keep the timetable going perfectly?
qa.a: Anand did it perfectly for nine days.

qa.q: What was Anand thinking when the late wedding made the morning session impossible?
qa.a: That one missed session had ruined everything, an all-or-nothing thought mixed with disappointment.

qa.q: What could Anand have done on the evening of day ten?
qa.a: Anand could have opened the laptop for even twenty minutes so the routine kept going.

qa.q: How might Parveen react to hearing this confession?
qa.a: Parveen might recognise a few January plans of the same kind and would probably see Anand as honest rather than lazy. 🙂

grounding: Illustrates a young adult whose ambitious study routine ended after the first missed day because of all-or-nothing thinking.

passage: Our exams ran from the fourth to the fourteenth, and I watched Chaitanya prepare like someone laying bricks. A week before, he pinned a calendar above his desk: heavy days shaded red, one blank Sunday, and the four days after the last paper marked "nothing". During the exams he studied until ten and then switched off his lamp, even while the rest of us were still panicking in the corridor. On the blank Sunday he played football and came back muddy and hungry. When the exams were over, he slept, cooked with his mother and only opened a book on the fourth day, lightly. I cannot say what he was thinking. But he was the only one of us who walked into the last paper looking awake, and the only one who was not ill afterwards. Uma

qa.q: What did Chaitanya mark on the calendar for the four days after the last paper?
qa.a: The four days after the last paper were marked "nothing".

qa.q: What might Chaitanya have been feeling when he switched off the lamp at ten while others panicked?
qa.a: Probably calm and confident in the plan, though Uma cannot be sure and only saw the behaviour.

qa.q: What could a panicking friend learn from Chaitanya's calendar?
qa.a: Plan the hard days with rest days around them, and put recovery on the calendar before the exams begin.

qa.q: How might Uma have felt watching the others panic while Chaitanya switched off the lamp?
qa.a: Probably a mix of admiration and envy, since Uma noticed Chaitanya looked awake and was not ill afterwards.

grounding: Illustrates a student who accepts an intense exam phase but schedules rest before and after it, seen by a classmate.

passage: On Tuesday, Sahil drew two columns on the whiteboard for the college fest. "Sprint for the last ten days, then a slow week after," he told Wasim, his co-organiser, and he blocked the Monday after the fest as a holiday for the whole team. On the Friday of fest week, Sahil ran the stage checks until midnight, went to bed at one, and refused Wasim's offer to stay until three. "Tomorrow is the real day. Be in by eight." The following Wednesday, the volunteers sat in the canteen at four o'clock, laughing and doing nothing. Sahil had answered only two messages all week, and Wasim finally had time to fix the banner properly, unhurried. "We'll do the same next term," Sahil said, tapping the whiteboard, where the slow week was still written in green.

qa.q: What did Sahil block as a holiday for the whole team?
qa.a: Sahil blocked the Monday after the fest as a holiday for the whole team.

qa.q: What was Sahil probably feeling when he refused to let Wasim stay until three?
qa.a: Calm and protective of the team's energy, wanting everyone fresh for the real day.

qa.q: What did the plan get right about the last days before a big event?
qa.a: It put the hard push into a short window and set a recovery week after it, so the team could repeat the effort next term.

qa.q: How might Wasim have felt on the Wednesday with time to fix the banner unhurried?
qa.a: Relieved and rested, able to do the work properly rather than rushing while tired. 😊

grounding: Illustrates a thoughtful organiser who plans an intense phase for an event and a planned recovery week afterwards.

passage: Every morning at 6:40, before the pressure cooker whistled in the next flat, Uday opened his laptop in his Pune flat and practised spreadsheet formulas for thirty minutes. Some days he only rewrote yesterday's formula. A few days he wanted to stop, because nothing seemed to change. A year later, his manager asked who could clean the vendor data before Friday. Uma, who had done an eight-hour weekend course in March and forgotten most of it, looked hard at her screen. Uday said he could, opened a blank sheet and had the messy list sorted and checked by afternoon. Uma watched, then asked what time he started in the mornings. "Six-forty," he said. "Just half an hour. I stopped counting the days a long time ago.

qa.q: How long did Uday practise each morning?
qa.a: Uday practised for thirty minutes, starting at 6:40.

qa.q: What might Uday have felt on the days he wanted to stop?
qa.a: Doubtful and discouraged, because nothing seemed to change.

qa.q: What could someone like Uma take from that Friday?
qa.a: Pick a small practice, do it every day and stay with it long enough for results to show, instead of relying on one big course.

qa.q: How might Uma have felt when Uday cleaned the vendor data so quickly?
qa.a: Impressed, and perhaps a little uneasy, since her own eight-hour course had mostly faded. 😅

grounding: Illustrates a steady worker who practises a skill briefly every day and is far ahead a year later, unlike a one-off binge.

passage:
"You're sketching again? In the pantry, Gopika?"
"Thirty minutes, Arnab. Every lunch since last March."
"I did a whole weekend last month. Twelve hours. Then my wrist hurt and I stopped."
"Look at this. My first page." She turned her sketchbook back to the start, and he stared at the wobbly cups.
"That's yours?"
"And this is last week's." The cup now had a shadow and a curl of steam.
"Did you feel it getting better?"
"No. Some days I hated it. I only noticed when I flipped back."
"So it's just... every day."
"Every day. Boring and slow, but it adds up."
"Hm. I'll try tomorrow."
"Bring your own pencil."

qa.q: How long does Gopika sketch each lunch?
qa.a: Gopika sketches for thirty minutes, every lunch since last March.

qa.q: What did Gopika feel on some days while practising?
qa.a: Frustration: she says she hated it on some days and only saw the progress when she flipped back.

qa.q: What could Arnab do differently after seeing the two pages?
qa.a: Practise a little each day rather than one long weekend, so his wrist gets rest and progress builds up.

qa.q: What is it like for Arnab to compare his cups with Gopika's pages?
qa.a: He is probably surprised and a bit humbled, since the first page was so wobbly and the recent one has shadow and steam. 😅

grounding: Illustrates a steady worker whose thirty daily minutes add up to real skill over a year, while the results stay invisible for a long time.

subtype: Colleague who is reliable rather than brilliant [Observer]
passage: In the Berlin translation office, the Thursday report arrived at four o'clock, always from Selin, always short and clear. Kofi had watched it for months. Marek, the star of the team, had once turned around a whole client glossary overnight and everyone clapped, but then he vanished for two weeks and his tasks stayed open. When the big contract came, the team lead handed the schedule to Selin without much discussion. "I know she'll tell me on Thursday if something slips," the lead said. Nobody asked Marek. Kofi wondered whether Selin even knew how much trust had built up, week by week, out of small reports. Selin just nodded and opened the calendar.

qa.q: At what time did Selin's report arrive each Thursday?
qa.a: Selin's report arrived at four o'clock.

qa.q: What was Kofi feeling and wondering as the lead gave the schedule to Selin?
qa.a: Kofi felt quietly impressed and curious, wondering whether Selin knew how much trust the small weekly reports had built.

qa.q: What could a star like Marek do to earn the same trust?
qa.a: Deliver something small every week and say early when something slips, so the team can count on him.

qa.q: How might Selin experience being chosen without much discussion?
qa.a: Probably quietly pleased and maybe surprised, since the choice came from steady weekly habits and not from one big moment.

grounding: Illustrates a team noticing that a quiet team member's steady weekly delivery earns more trust than a star who disappears.

subtype: Colleague who is reliable rather than brilliant [Observer]
passage: In the staff room of the city school, Madhav counted the Monday sheets pinned to the board: eleven in a row from Indu, each with attendance and pending fees in the same neat columns. Rohit, the art teacher, had painted the whole annual-day backdrop in one weekend and got applause, but for the next fortnight his register stayed blank and other teachers covered his classes. When the principal needed someone to plan the exam duty roster, she looked at the board, then at Indu. "You have never missed a Monday," she said. Indu blinked, then tucked her pen away. That evening Madhav took out his own diary and wrote down one small thing he could deliver every single week.

qa.q: How many Monday sheets did Madhav count on the board?
qa.a: Madhav counted eleven Monday sheets in a row from Indu.

qa.q: What was Madhav feeling as he wrote one small weekly commitment in his diary?
qa.a: Inspired and a little self-critical, having seen steady delivery earn trust. 😊

qa.q: What could Rohit do to become as trusted as Indu?
qa.a: Rohit could make small regular contributions, such as keeping his register filled every week, and not only big weekend bursts.

qa.q: How might Indu have felt when the principal mentioned the Monday sheets?
qa.a: Surprised, as the blink shows, and possibly pleased to learn that the steady sheets counted.

grounding: Illustrates colleagues noticing that the quiet person delivering every week is trusted over the star who vanishes and reappears.

passage: On the community-centre wall chart, Chinmay's row had one empty box, Tuesday. Bidisha, who ran the morning walking club, pointed at it. "You missed." "Train got in at midnight," Chinmay said. "So on Wednesday I did the minimum: laced up, walked to the gate and back. Five minutes. Box ticked." He had used the same trick in his sister's wedding week and during a bad cold, when the minimum was stretching by the window. "The rule is, miss one, fine. Never two." Bidisha looked at the chart again. On Thursday his usual forty minutes came back without any argument. By March his row had three lone gaps and no double ones, and half the club had copied the idea, each with a minimum of their own.

qa.q: Which day was the empty box in Chinmay's row?
qa.a: The empty box was on Tuesday.

qa.q: What was Chinmay feeling as he ticked the box after only five minutes on Wednesday?
qa.a: Relieved and steady, since the chain stayed alive without needing a perfect day. 🙂

qa.q: What could someone with an unpredictable schedule borrow from Chinmay?
qa.a: Set a tiny minimum version for bad days, and allow one miss but never two in a row.

qa.q: How might Bidisha have seen the chart differently by March?
qa.a: At first the empty box looked like a slip, but by March it showed the rule working, with only single gaps and half the club copying it.

grounding: Illustrates a habit-builder who tolerates one missed day, keeps a five-minute minimum for bad days and never misses twice.

passage:
Dear Jasleen,
You asked how the writing streak survived the conference trip. Honestly, barely. On Monday my flight landed at 2 a.m. and I skipped my usual page. Fine, I told myself. On Tuesday I was exhausted and the hotel Wi-Fi kept dropping, but I had promised myself I would not miss twice. So I opened the notebook in the taxi and wrote one line about the driver's radio. That was it. One sentence, ticked. On Wednesday I felt better and wrote the full page without forcing it. On the flight home I counted: forty-one pages since January, one missed day, nothing else. Bad days used to end my plans; now the small version holds the chain together. Come over on Sunday and I will show you the notebook.
Deepika

qa.q: What did Deepika write in the taxi on Tuesday?
qa.a: Deepika wrote one line about the driver's radio.

qa.q: What was Deepika feeling on Tuesday when promising not to miss twice?
qa.a: Tired but determined, exhausted yet resolved to keep the chain going.

qa.q: What small step helped Deepika keep the streak alive on a bad day?
qa.a: Writing one sentence, a minimum version, so the day still counted.

qa.q: How might Jasleen feel reading about the streak?
qa.a: Probably curious and impressed, and maybe inspired to try a small habit, given the invitation to see the notebook.

grounding: Illustrates a habit-builder who accepts one missed day but keeps a one-sentence minimum so no second day is missed.

passage: In the village near Sikar, Yamini decided that sleep was for people who did not want the scholarship test. She set her alarm for 3 a.m., skipped the evening walk to the well with her brother Irfan and ate lunch with the book propped against her plate. By the second week, the formulas she had learnt slid away by afternoon and she read the same paragraph four times. On the mock test she left two easy questions blank, then cried over the paper. Irfan found her on the veranda step. "You look like the lamp when the oil is low," he said. That night she slept until six, and the next day the paragraph made sense in one read.

qa.q: What time did Yamini set her alarm for?
qa.a: Yamini set her alarm for 3 a.m.

qa.q: How was Yamini feeling on the veranda step after the mock test?
qa.a: Upset and frustrated, since she cried over the blank answers even though she was working harder than ever.

qa.q: What could Yamini try to protect her studying?
qa.a: Sleep at regular hours and keep short breaks such as the evening walk, so that what she learns stays with her.

qa.q: How might Irfan see his sister's new routine?
qa.a: With worry; the lamp remark shows he sees her running low on energy.

grounding: Illustrates a teenager preparing for an entrance test who cuts sleep and breaks, then finds memory and concentration falling.

passage: Yosef pinned a note above his bed in Lyon: Wake at 4:30. He had worked out that sleeping until seven cost him two and a half hours a day, and he was not going to lose them before the entrance test in June. He skipped breaks too, eating bread at his desk. After ten days he could not recall the rule he had studied on Monday, and twice he left his keys in the door. In the mock test he wrote the wrong term where the answer needed the discriminant. His study partner Clara pushed the marked paper across the table. "You knew this in March," she said. Yosef felt strangely proud of the tiredness, as if it proved something, but he did not answer, and later set the alarm for six.

qa.q: What time did Yosef's note say to wake?
qa.a: The note said to wake at 4:30.

qa.q: What did Yosef feel about the tiredness even as his marks fell?
qa.a: Strangely proud, as if it proved something, yet uneasy enough to move his alarm to six.

qa.q: What could Yosef do with the extra hours he wants?
qa.a: Protect his sleep and take breaks so that what he studies stays in memory; short rested sessions beat long tired ones.

qa.q: How does Clara see Yosef's studying?
qa.a: With concern; reminding him that he knew the material in March shows she sees the tiredness costing him.

grounding: Illustrates a teenager who gives up sleep and breaks for exam hours and sees memory and performance drop while the sacrifice still feels virtuous.

passage:
From the next room, I have heard Vijay's alarm every morning for three years. This term it rings and rings. Vijay used to bring the group's notes to my door every Sunday, with jokes; now the notes have stopped, and when I asked about the internship report the answer was, "Who even reads them?" Vijay sleeps a full night and still has a face like Monday at midnight. Vijay skipped my birthday dinner and did not text back, which never happened before. I cannot say what is going on inside. I knocked, put a cup of tea on the desk and said, "This term looks heavy. Is it the load, or something else?" Vijay looked up. "Maybe just the load." We sat for a while, and I suggested speaking to our faculty mentor about dropping something.
Sarika

qa.q: What did Sarika put on Vijay's desk?
qa.a: Sarika put a cup of tea on Vijay's desk.

qa.q: What might Vijay be feeling, judging by the cues Sarika describes?
qa.a: Drained and detached, suggested by the flat "Who even reads them?", the unanswered texts and the skipped dinner, though Sarika cannot be sure.

qa.q: What did Sarika suggest, and why is it sensible?
qa.a: Speaking to the faculty mentor about dropping something, since lightening the load early is a reasonable response to lasting tiredness.

qa.q: How might Sarika have felt when Vijay stopped answering texts?
qa.a: Worried and a little hurt, which fits with knocking and bringing tea.

grounding: Illustrates a student who is tired despite resting and cares less about things that once mattered, noticed and gently asked by the person in the next room.

passage: On Monday, Hafsa slept nine hours and woke as tired as before. In the seminar she thought, what is the point of any of this? and did not finish a reading she once loved. On Thursday she skipped the literacy club she had started, then found a thank-you card for her mentor still unsigned in her bag from two weeks ago and pushed it deeper. She felt guilty for not caring. That night her roommate Gurleen said, "You're not ungrateful. You're carrying too much." The next Tuesday the two of them sat with the academic advisor, and Hafsa put down the list of her five commitments. She dropped one course and handed the club to a junior. By Friday she still felt flat, but she had slept and eaten lunch away from her laptop.

qa.q: How many hours did Hafsa sleep on Monday?
qa.a: Hafsa slept nine hours and woke as tired as before.

qa.q: What was Hafsa feeling about herself when she pushed the unsigned card deeper into her bag?
qa.a: Guilty for not caring, and flat and cynical about things that once mattered.

qa.q: What could Hafsa do if she still feels flat after these changes?
qa.a: Keep reducing her load, and if it keeps going or worries her, check with a doctor or a counsellor.

qa.q: How does Gurleen see Hafsa's behaviour?
qa.a: As a sign of too much load rather than ingratitude, since Gurleen tells Hafsa she is carrying too much.

grounding: Illustrates a student who feels cynical, tired despite rest and uncaring, and whose signs point to an unsustainable load and not to weakness.

passage:
Subject: Not sure when it changed
Dear Ganga,
Nobody in my team has ever told me to answer messages at night. That is the strange part. But when the lead replies at 11:30 p.m., I find my phone in my hand within a minute. Last Saturday I answered four threads before breakfast, and a small voice said, they are all awake, do not be the one who is not. Sundays now start with a knot. I used to build small clocks from scrap on weekends; that box has been shut since March and I cannot even remember why I liked it. This week I told my lead I would reply by ten in the morning on weekends, and to my surprise the answer was just "ok". I do not know if that helps yet. How did you cope at your old firm?
Santosh

qa.q: When does the lead reply at night?
qa.a: The lead replies at 11:30 p.m.

qa.q: What does Santosh feel on Sundays, and why?
qa.a: A knot of dread, because the week's messages and the unspoken expectation to answer them come back.

qa.q: What did Santosh try, and what could come next?
qa.a: Santosh told the lead about replying by ten on weekends; a next step could be protecting one evening and talking further with the lead.

qa.q: How might Ganga read this email?
qa.a: With sympathy, since Santosh asks how Ganga coped at an old firm, which suggests Ganga may have seen this kind of culture before.

grounding: Illustrates an employee who slowly loses rest and interest because of unspoken expectations to reply at night and on weekends.

passage: Varun, listen, you know me, Vaibhav, I never complain about work. It is not like my boss ever said "reply at midnight". It is the little stuff. Someone posts "anyone free?" on the team chat at nine on Saturday night, and three thumbs-up land within two minutes. Then it is mine to answer, or I am the one who did not. Last month I caught myself checking the chat at my cousin's engagement, out in the corridor. My sleep has gone thin, and the dashboards I used to enjoy building? I open them and feel nothing. Yesterday I realised I had not been to the badminton court in two months. I do not know how it got here, and no single day did it. Do you think it is me being soft, or is this how it starts?

qa.q: What lands within two minutes after "anyone free?" is posted?
qa.a: Three thumbs-up land within two minutes.

qa.q: What is Vaibhav worried about at the end?
qa.a: Vaibhav worries whether this is personal softness or a pressure that builds up slowly, and feels drained and uninterested.

qa.q: What small first step could Vaibhav take?
qa.a: Ask the team lead how urgent late weekend messages really are, or set a quiet evening, and go back to the badminton court.

qa.q: How might Varun respond to being asked whether Vaibhav is being soft?
qa.a: Varun might reassure Vaibhav that slow exhaustion is common and not softness, and encourage a talk with a manager.

grounding: Illustrates an employee whose rest and interest erode through unspoken late-night and weekend expectations, not one order.

passage: At the milk cooperative office in a small Maharashtra town, Irawati watched Parveen snap at the weighing clerk over a missing sticker, something she had never done in four years. Twice that week the ledger showed wrong totals, and Parveen no longer joined the tea circle at eleven. Irawati said nothing in front of the others. Instead, after closing on Thursday, she asked, "Walk with me to the bus stop?" On the way she said, "You have seemed worn out lately. I am not asking for details, only whether I can take the Saturday totals off you." Parveen's eyes filled, and she nodded. Irawati checked the totals, and the next Monday she said that if the tiredness kept going or worried her, it was worth seeing a doctor.

qa.q: Where did Irawati ask Parveen to walk with her?
qa.a: Irawati asked Parveen to walk with her to the bus stop after closing on Thursday.

qa.q: What might Irawati have been feeling when she noticed Parveen snapping and making errors?
qa.a: Concerned and careful, which is why she chose to speak privately.

qa.q: Why was the walk to the bus stop a better choice than a remark in the tea circle?
qa.a: A private, caring word avoids embarrassing Parveen in front of others and makes it easier to accept help.

qa.q: What is it like for Parveen when Irawati offers to take the Saturday totals?
qa.a: A relief and an emotional moment; Parveen's eyes fill, which shows she was carrying more than she said.

grounding: Illustrates a coworker noticing irritability, careless errors and withdrawal and offering a private check-in and a suggestion to see a doctor.

passage: Ingrid noticed it first on the tram: Priscila, usually chatty, stared out of the window with her headphones on. In the office the pattern grew. Priscila corrected a colleague with a sharp sigh at Tuesday's meeting, sent a report with the wrong month in the title and ate lunch alone at her desk. Ingrid did not raise it in the group chat. On Friday she wrote, "Coffee downstairs at three? No agenda." Over the cups she said, "You seem stretched thin. I am not judging." Priscila was quiet, then said she had not slept well for weeks. Ingrid mentioned the company's confidential support line and offered to sit with her while she called.

qa.q: What was wrong with the report Priscila sent?
qa.a: The report had the wrong month in the title.

qa.q: What might Ingrid have been feeling as she chose not to raise it in the group chat?
qa.a: Concerned and careful, wanting to protect Priscila's dignity.

qa.q: What could Priscila do if the poor sleep keeps going?
qa.a: Call the confidential support line, with Ingrid beside her, or check with a doctor.

qa.q: What is it like for Priscila to be invited for coffee with no agenda?
qa.a: Probably a relief and less pressure than being called out in a group; she was quiet at first, then opened up about her sleep.

grounding: Illustrates a coworker noticing irritability, careless errors and withdrawal and choosing a private check-in and pointing to professional support.
